content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper integrates a 2D Haar-Wavelet into CNN-like networks as a new "Wave-Mix-Lite" block. The goal is to reduce the resource requirements of the architecture (such that training on a single GPU becomes feasible). The paper claims that the new architecture is better transferable to new computer vision tasks and presents results of the method for image classifi�cation (e.g. ImageNet) and semantic segmentation (Cityscapes). The paper claims competitive performance on several benchmarks. Claims regarding scale-invariance of the method are also made.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**
* The paper addresses an important topic: how to reduce the computational requirements for model training and inference for modern computer vision architectures.
* The presented architecture is easy to understand and deserves to be investigated.
* The combination of the classical Haar Wavelet with modern architectures is an interesting approach.

**Weaknesses**
* In my opinion the experiments are not sufficient to support what is claimed in the paper, nor do they enable the reader to understand in what way the approach can be considered competitive.
* The comparisons made in the paper remain somewhat unclear and the ablation studies are also lacking in clarity and scope.

Details on Weaknesses:

The fact that no image augmentations were used is a significant weakness in my opinion. This makes the results incomparable to a large fraction of the published literature and much less interesting. It is not clear how the observed differences in performance would change with augmentations. Augmentation can also act as a regularizer, so comparing other regularization methods would then be important.

How were the hyperparameters chosen? How much tuning of the hyperparameters was done for the proposed and the compared methods? Without understanding these questions, the comparisons presented are very hard to judge for the reader, because optimal parameters may vary widely based on the method.

The 2D Haar DWT could be implemented as a stride-2 2x2 convolution. A very natural ablation would be to replace the DWT in the WaveMix block by a convolution and (a) train from scratch or (b) train by initializing with the Haar coefficients. If I understand Section 3.2 correctly, then even not training this part of the network could lead to a speed-up.

The paper claims that "For training ImageNet-1K, we used the ResNets, MobileNets and ViT models available in pytorch library". It is then surprising to me that the results are so far off some of the published results of e.g ResNets on ImageNet. I thought that reaching >70% accuracy on ImageNet with a plain ResNet should be possible. 

Apart from the ImageNet results, also results on other datasets for classification are far from what the literature seems to consider state of the art. E.g. (Table 6 vs. papers-with-code, no external data) CIFAR-10 93% vs. ~98%; CIFAR-100 70% vs ~89%; TinyImNet 55% vs. ~70%. If there are reasons why the authors believe that the comparisons are still fair, and current SOTA should "not count", this should be made clearer. (E.g. why augmentation cannot be used here or what the exact inference or training time restriction is and why that is the right number.) 

For Places-365 the authors claim SOTA accuracy at 56.45%, while even the original paper (TPAMI 2017) that introduced the dataset already presented accuracies of >55%. It would be good to explain this further (I only found very few comparison results). 

Overall, it would be great to understand the uncertainty of the measurements presented in the tables.

The argument that "WaveMix-Lite can be directly used for semantic segmentation" is not very convincing to me unless there are comparison to similar architectures that also avoid a down-scaling of the results with increasing depth.

It is possible that the authors might not have taken into account the differences in the ResNet families for ImageNet (224 scale, ResNet18/34/50/...) and CIFAR (ResNet20/32/44/56). This is not clear from the paper, because so many variants of ResNets exist, but it should be clarified.

Minor point: It is not clear to me why the DWT is considered to be "token-mixing". As far as I'm aware, the DWT used here has a very local receptive field.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: good; the paper is mostly easy to read.

Quality: not convincing; see "weaknesses" above.

Novelty: limited; the use of the DWT is interesting but very closely related to convolutions, so without convincing experimental results, the novelty remains limited in my opinion.

Reproducibility: Good; if the authors publish their code as promised, the results are very likely reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: There are major concerns regarding how much the claims are supported by the experiments, hence the paper should not be accepted to ICLR in my opinion.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths::
1) Given the increased used of CNNs in embedded systems this type of research should be pursued with more importance.
2) Additionally, the motivation for designing the proposed method in section 3 is nicely mentioned.

Weaknesses::
The paper can be improved based on the following points.
1) The introduction section (section 1) seems to be lacking motivational case study. Please provide an example to motivate the users to keep reading, especially why the proposed method is important.
2) Section 3, lacks generalisation of the proposed architecture. The proposed architecture specifies what design choices were made but it fails to mention why such design choices were made for individual components. Please specify. Also, Try to generalise the architecture by using mathematical formulas such that the proposed could be utilised in a broader sense.
3) In section 1, comparative study though extensive but lacks strategy for comparison. One of the key factors the proposed architecture is compared is its computational efficiency but that is not provided in the comparative study. Only Top 1 Accuracy, total GPU RAM usage or number of parameters are evaluated however, an important criteria would be the energy consumption and/or total training time in such evaluation. However, these results were missing. Please provide them as necessary by choosing a particular hardware platform to provide a comprehensive comparative study for the mentioned criteria.
4) Section 4 could be arranged better. Implementation details came after comparative study which made it difficult to read. Please rearrange the subsections of this section accordingly to improve readability.
5) I would suggest to segregate conclusion section from discussion and future direction for better readability.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a new architecture – WaveMix-Lite – that can generalize on par with contemporary transformers and convolutional neural networks while needing fewer resources. In particular, WaveMix-Lite uses 2D-discrete wavelet transform to efficiently mix spatial information from pixels. Extensive experiments on image classification and semantic segmentation tasks have shown the effectiveness of WaveMix-Lite.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
 1. The  WaveMix-Lite can capture two kinds of priors, i.e., multiresolution self-similarity and sparseness of edges.

 2. WaveMix-Lite does not require significant architectural changes, as compared with CNNs or  Transformers.

Weaknesses:

1. The novelty is limited，many prior works have applied the discrete wavelet transforms in the application of deep neural networks.

2. The experiment is invalid，large datasets， such as ImageNet or COCO，should be considered.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity, quality and reproducibility are good, my major concern is about the novelty.
content.summary_of_the_review:
1. The novelty is limited，we find that many prior works have applied the discrete wavelet transforms in the application of deep neural networks. Please discuss the difference or advantage of WaveMix-Lite.

  [1] Chakraborty J, Nandy A. Discrete wavelet transform based data representation in deep neural network for gait abnormality detection[J]. 
       Biomedical Signal Processing and Control, 2020, 62: 102076.
  [2] Sarhan A M. Brain tumor classification in magnetic resonance images using deep learning and wavelet transform[J]. Journal of 
       Biomedical Science and Engineering, 2020, 13(06): 102.
  [3] Li Q, Shen L. WaveSNet: Wavelet integrated deep networks for image segmentation[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2005.14461, 2020.

2. The Discrete Fourier Transform has been widely used In Deep Neutral Network，which can also keep multiresolution self-similarity and sparseness of edges. Please explain the difference between Discrete Fourier Transform and Discrete Wavelet Transforms.

3. The current datasets are small to evaluate the effectiveness of WaveMix-Lite. If possible, please evaluate the WaveMix-Lite on large datasets, such as ImageNet or COCO.
 
4. In Table 1, considering the Top-1 Accuracy, Parameter， GPU RAM，the WaveMix-Lite can not achieved the best performance.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes integrating two-dimensional fast wavelet transforms with static Haar filters into convolutional neural networks.
The proposed "Wave-Mix-Lite"-blocks contain concatenation, some learned operations, and end with a batch norm operation followed by a residual connection. 
The proposed method is evaluated on then ImageNet-1K, MNIST, Fashion MNIST classification data sets and the Cityscapes segmentation problem.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Paper strengths:
-  Wavelet transforms are a classic technique in signal processing. Reviving the use of wavelets via integration into CNN is interesting.
- In a world with finite resources reducing the computational cost of modern neural networks is essential.

Paper Weaknesses:
- The paper contains misleading statements. A single-scale 2D-DWT runs four convolutions. This fact should be mentioned when comparing it to convolutional layers with learned filters.
- Generally, the paper presents weak baselines the datasets used are comparatively small, and the ablation study is not convincing.
- The experimental part considers only the very basic Haar wavelet.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
## Clarity and Quality:
The text contains misleading statements and leaves many questions open. A selection of open points:

### Introduction and Methods:
- Abstract: The fast wavelet transform is computed via convolutions. In comparison to traditional CNN layers the filters are fixed. Why would traditional CNN-layers struggle with scale invariance or the "finite spatial extend of objects"?

- Page 1: CNN generalize better than which alternatives in particular?

- Is it really fair to call the Haar wavelet a special case of the Daubechies-wavelet family? Technically its true, but the Haar wavelet has only two entries per filter and is much simpler than any other  Daubechies-wavelet.

- Page 4: Page 4 states, "This is where the wavelet transform plays its role in both increasing the effective receptive field at an exponential rate per layer (unlike the linear rate of convolutional layers)". The fast wavelet transform is computed using stride two convolutions with fixed filters. How could the growth of the receptive field possibly be different compared to convolutional layers which use the same operation and a filter learned via gradient descent?

- Page 5: Section 3.2 states, "Since wavelet transform reduces the image resolution by half, the GPU consumption and computations needed by the MLP significantly reduces in each layer."
What does the transposed conv layer from Figure 1 do? Typically transposed convolutions contain an upsampling operation which would undo the downsampling effect the 2D-DWT had.

- Page 7: In section 4.4 it seems the 2D-DWT is considered as a single operation. The section states: "Even though a single convolutional operation is comparatively cheaper than
a 2D-DWT, we can achieve generalization comparable to deep convolutional networks with far
fewer layers of the wavelet transforms." The sentence could mislead readers, because a level 1 2D-DWT uses four convolutions. Esentially the 2D-DWT increases the width with fixed filters. The notion presented here seems counterintitive since i.e. https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/mlp.html found better depth to help in figure 6.7.


### Experiments:
- Have wavelets other than the Haar wavelet been explored?
- What about transfer learning using networks pre-trained on the full imagenet?
- The baselines in the ablation study are not convincing:
  - Four learned stride-two convolutions should have replaced the 2D-FWT instead of removing it altogether.
  - The 2D Fourier transform allows downsampling. [Rippel2015] for example, achieved Fourier-downsampling by center-cropping the transformed image. Since the transformation of real-valued inputs is hermitian. The real- and imaginary- parts could have been concatenated along the channel dimension for a fair comparison.

[Rippel2015] Rippel, Oren, Jasper Snoek, and Ryan P. Adams. "Spectral representations for convolutional neural networks." Advances in neural information processing systems 28 (2015).

- Haar-wavelets are one-dimensional. How can a one-dimensional wavelet work in a two-dimensional convolution?

### Appendix:
- The appendix states: "Each increment in the level of 2D-DWT results in doubling of the number
of parameters, but provides only a very small reduction in GPU consumption, especially when we
go to higher levels of 2D-DWT." Where are the "additional" parameters coming from?

## Novelty:
The downsampling aspect of the 2D-FWT was previously observed by Williams et al (https://openreview.net/pdf?id=rkhlb8lCZ). This observation is not novel.  The authors may want to add a citation.


## Reproducibility:
Mean and standard deviations are unknown for all experiments. Without the seeds, the numbers will be hard to reproduce.
content.summary_of_the_review: For an experimental paper exploring the wavelet transform in CNN, working only with small datasets using only the haar wavelet is not enough. The ablation study is problematic, and the novelty is limited since the pooling aspect has already been observed by Williams et al (https://openreview.net/pdf?id=rkhlb8lCZ), who are not cited.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
